items.title: For members of sexual and gender minorities, trauma therapies work best when adapted to their realities, study suggests
items.text: When therapies for psychological trauma are adapted for sexual and gender minorities and delivered by therapists with high levels of sensitivity to their experiences, outcomes are better, according to a scoping review by McGill University researchers. In particular, there are fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms such as nightmares and intrusive thoughts, as well as risk-taking behaviors (e.g., self-harm, drug use), the researchers said.

items.title: Potentially deadly soil bacterium gaining foothold in new regions, including the US
items.text: A potentially deadly disease caused by a soil-dwelling bacterium long found in tropical regions may be slowly gaining a foothold in the continental United States and other regions around the world. The discovery of the bacterium in Mississippi is raising new questions about how doctors should identify infections and track its spread.

items.title: Small daily activities may help ease dementia caregivers' stress
items.text: Nearly 12 million people in the U.S. provide unpaid care to a relative or friend with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Compared with caregivers of people without dementia, ADRD caregivers face greater demands that may contribute to higher rates of depression, anxiety, sleep problems, reduced physical activity and chronic illness.

items.title: GLP-1 drugs show lower obesity-related cancer risk than insulin, but not all diabetes treatments
items.text: Years of research point to obesity and type 2 diabetes raising the risk of developing several types of cancer. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a recent medical breakthrough, were originally developed for blood sugar control or diabetes management and also work overtime promoting weight loss. Scientists are curious to explore whether there are any links between these drugs and the onset of cancers in people with diabetes.

items.title: Very strong El Niño episodes are associated with over 100,000 additional heat-related deaths worldwide per year
items.text: The current El Niño episode, often described as a "super El Niño," raises concerns about the potential impact of this phenomenon on global temperatures and related health impacts. A new study by the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal) has examined the relationship between this climate phenomenon and temperature-related mortality worldwide. The study, published in Nature Medicine, estimates that very strong El Niño episodes are associated with 107,035 additional heat-related deaths and 112,681 fewer cold-related deaths per year compared with neutral conditions.

items.title: How odor can signify unsafe water consumption
items.text: Learning to associate certain food smells with unpleasant ailments following consumption helps many organisms learn which foods are unsafe. In a new study in JNeurosci, Dan Rokni and colleagues at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem used mice to explore how the brain learns that some smells signify "unsafe to ingest." The researchers focused on the role of the nucleus of the lateral olfactory tract (NLOT), which supports communication between the nose and the brain about smells.
